question: to the Commission Jean-Paul Garraud (PfE) Subject:

Under the principle of subsidiarity enshrined in the EU’s Treaties, national parliaments have the right to point out instances of a European project unnecessarily encroaching upon the Member States’ competences. They only have eight weeks to react, however, and their objections rarely oblige the Commission to withdraw its text. The early warning mechanism provided for in Protocol No 2 to the Treaty on European Union aims to ensure compliance with the principle of subsidiarity by directly involving national parliaments in the scrutiny of EU legislative proposals. In practice, despite the fact that this ‘yellow card’ mechanism has been used on a number of occasions, it has very rarely led to a Commission proposal being substantially amended or withdrawn. This raises questions as how effective the mechanism actually is. 1.
Is the Commission in favour of giving national parliaments more time to scrutinise proposed EU legislation so that they can fully exercise the subsidiarity check provided for in the Treaties?

Will it agree to a mandatory review of a proposal when a significant number of national parliaments take the view that the EU is reaching beyond its remit, and to provide a detailed statement of the reasons behind any decision to maintain its proposal despite those objections?
Would it support a mechanism that allows the national parliaments to have a proposal for EU legislation withdrawn when a majority of the national parliaments object to it?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) 1. The deadline of eight weeks for national Parliaments’ subsidiarity check of proposed EU legislation is set in Article 6 of Protocol No 21 to the Treaties. To facilitate national Parliaments’ scrutiny during recess periods, the Commission excludes the periods from 1 to 31 August and from 20 December to 10 January of the following year from the calculation of the eight weeks. Any change of the eight weeks deadline would require a Treaty revision, in which the European Parliament and the Member States play a key role. 2. The thresholds for triggering a review by the Commission of a draft legislative act are described in Article 7(2) of Protocol No 22. After a review, the Commission may decide to maintain, amend or withdraw the draft. Reasons must be given for this decision. Further than that, the Commission has committed to provide a detailed and comprehensive ‘aggregated response’ to the subsidiarity concerns expressed by a significant number of national Parliaments even if the number of their reasoned opinions does not reach the relevant thresholds for triggering a review set in Protocol No 2. 3. Article 7(3) of Protocol No 2 gives to the European Parliament and the Council, as the Union legislator, the right to decide whether a legislative proposal shall be given further consideration after a majority of national Parliaments has considered it as being in breach with the subsidiarity principle but the Commission decided to maintain it. Giving the same right to national Parliaments would require a Treaty change.
1 Protocol (No 2) on the application of the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality, https://eur-

lex.europa.eu/LexUriServ/LexUriServ.do?uri=CELEX:12008M/PRO/02:EN:HTML. 2 Reasoned opinions on a draft legislative act's non-compliance with the principle of subsidiarity representing at least one third of the votes allocated to national Parliaments, or one quarter for proposals in the area of freedom, security and justice based on Article 76 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
